comparison: Perfect agreement on disease association and clinical characterization (C2-C6, C58-C61). Both evaluations support the clinical phenotypes and structural locations with appropriate citations. OpenEval emphasizes consistency with SNARE architecture while peer reviewers acknowledge these as established disease-causing mutations.

Strong agreement on in vitro biochemical assays (C7-C9, C92, C100-C102). Both recognize the in vitro work as a major strength extending beyond prior studies. Peer reviewers explicitly praise the ability to control experimental variables in purified systems, aligning with OpenEval's assessment of consistent functional deficits across multiple independent assays.

Agreement on electrophysiology findings (C65-C67) and co-expression experiments (C68-C69). Both support the gain-of-function interpretation with increased spontaneous release exceeding Syt1 KO. OpenEval notes incomplete dominance mechanism requires further investigation, while peer reviewers accept the comparison to Syt1 KO as supporting gain-of-function.

Complete agreement on evoked release measurements (C70-C77). Both evaluations accept the desynchronization phenotype and the comparison to Syt1 KO. Peer reviewers confirm these findings align with prior work while showing distinct features, matching OpenEval's conclusion about mutations having effects beyond simple loss of Syt1 binding.

Agreement on RRP size reduction and energy barrier findings (C10-C12, C78-C86). Both recognize this as a key finding differing from prior work. Peer reviewers explicitly accept the gain-of-function interpretation and energy barrier model, aligning with OpenEval's assessment of reduced RRP and altered energy barriers with consistent potency ranking.

Agreement on kinetic modeling approach (C13-C14, C87-C90). Both evaluations recognize modeling as a strength. Peer reviewers praise the combination of electrophysiology, biophysics, and modeling for deeper mechanistic understanding, consistent with OpenEval's assessment of sound mathematical framework with justified simplifications.

Agreement on gain-of-function mechanism (C19-C20, C96-C99). Both support increased SNARE interactions and impaired complexin clamping. Peer reviewers explicitly endorse the gain-of-function interpretation for V48F/D166Y, aligning with OpenEval's assessment of direct demonstration through co-flotation and fusion assays.

Agreement on I67N phenotype (C21-C23, C107-C109). Both accept dramatic decreases in release and dominant-negative behavior. Peer reviewers characterize I67N as disrupting SNARE assembly/stability and acting as dominant-negative, consistent with OpenEval's assessment, though OpenEval notes qualification needed regarding RRP measurement methodology.

Agreement on I67N fusion barrier interpretation (C24, C110-C115). Both accept that I67N increases fusion energy barrier without affecting priming. Peer reviewers explicitly summarize this distinction, aligning with OpenEval's assessment of elegant demonstration through sucrose titration representing key mechanistic distinction from V48F/D166Y.

Agreement on charge rescue experiments (C25, C116-C118). Both support the evidence that I67N defect relates to energy barrier modulated by electrostatic forces. Peer reviewers implicitly endorse through positive assessment of mechanistic work, consistent with OpenEval's strong evidence assessment and differential rescue interpretation.

Agreement on mutation classification and energy landscape framework (C15-C18, C26, C119-C122). Both endorse the classification of mutations as having distinct mechanisms (gain-of-function vs. dominant-negative). Peer reviewers explicitly accept the loss- and gain-of-function properties and energy landscape effects, matching OpenEval's integration of evidence into coherent framework.

Partial overlap on gain-of-function conclusions (C15-C18). Both support gain-of-function interpretation through Syt1 KO comparison. OpenEval focuses on convergence of multiple measurements and potency ranking, while peer reviewers incorporate this into broader classification framework of mutation mechanisms.

Agreement on expression and survival data (C105-C106). Both accept western blot and survival findings as supporting functional studies. Peer reviewers implicitly endorse through lack of criticism and positive technical assessment, consistent with OpenEval's characterization as straightforward experimental observations.

Partial overlap on neuronal rescue experiments (C62-C64). Both accept functional expression demonstration. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of rescue experiments, electrophysiology, and co-expression, while peer reviewers address expression controls more briefly as part of overall technical quality endorsement.

Disagreement on interpretation of discrepancy with prior work (C53, C56). OpenEval supports current findings and attributes discrepancy to methodological differences. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting the RRP size discrepancy remains unresolved and could reflect both technical differences and model system differences.

Minor overlap on in vitro summary (C103). OpenEval provides specific summary claim integrating findings C100-C102. Peer reviewers address broader in vitro work (C93-C95 additionally) with emphasis on extension beyond prior studies and control of experimental variables.

OpenEval supports background claims on SNARE machinery and synaptic transmission (C1, C27-C34) as well-established literature context. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as peer reviewers focused on novel experimental findings rather than background knowledge.

OpenEval supports extensive background claims on SNAP25 function and regulation (C35-C52) as appropriately cited literature providing study rationale. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as peer reviewers did not separately assess background literature claims.
